records.source: וַיִּשְׁמַ֞ע הַכְּנַעֲנִ֤י מֶֽלֶךְ־עֲרָד֙ יֹשֵׁ֣ב הַנֶּ֔גֶב כִּ֚י בָּ֣א יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל דֶּ֖רֶךְ הָאֲתָרִ֑ים וַיִּלָּ֨חֶם֙ בְּיִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל וַיִּ֥שְׁבְּ׀מִמֶּ֖נּוּ שֶֽׁבִי׃
records.gloss: And heard the Canaanite, king of Arad, dwelling [in] the Negev, that had come Israel [by the] way of the Atharim; and he fought against Israel and took captive from it captive[s].
pieces: When the Canaanite king of Arad, who lived in the Negev, heard that Israel was coming along the Atharim road, he attacked Israel and took some of them prisoner.

L.1: And the Canaanite, the king of Arad, who lived in the Negev, heard that Israel had come by the way of Atharim; and he fought against Israel and took some of them captive.

R.1: The Canaanite king of Arad lived in the Negev, the dry country in the south. He heard that Israel was coming along the Atharim road. So he attacked the Israelites and captured some of them.

decisions.choice: Arad in the Negev: a Canaanite town in the dry south of the land
decisions.reason: The Negev is the dry country south of the hill country of Judah. Arad lay in its northern part (Joshua 12:14; Judges 1:16). Its king blocked Israel's way into the land from the south, where Israel had been beaten back before (14:44-45).

decisions.choice: the way of Atharim: a road named after a place, Atharim
decisions.reason: Atharim is read here as a place name, a road known by the place it led to. The word is found nowhere else, and it could also be read as "the way of the spies", the route the spies took into the land (13:17-21). The place cannot be located today.

decisions.choice: the Canaanite, the king of Arad: one man, the king
decisions.reason: "The Canaanite" and "king of Arad" name the same person: the king is the subject of "heard", "fought" and "took captive". In 33:40 the same king is named again. "Canaanite" here is a general name for the people of the land.

decisions.choice: the dry country in the south
decisions.reason: Readable explains the place name Negev, which many readers will not know.

records.heading: Victory at Hormah

records.source: וַיִּדַּ֨ר יִשְׂרָאֵ֥ל נֶ֛דֶר לַֽיהוָ֖ה וַיֹּאמַ֑ר אִם־נָתֹ֨ן תִּתֵּ֜ן אֶת־הָעָ֤ם הַזֶּה֙ בְּיָדִ֔י וְהַֽחֲרַמְתִּ֖י אֶת־עָרֵיהֶֽם׃
records.gloss: And vowed Israel [a] vow to Yahweh and said, If giving you will give the people the this into my hand, and I will devote to destruction their cities.
pieces: Then Israel made a vow to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}: "If {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} will truly hand this people over to us, we will devote their towns to destruction."

L.2: And Israel vowed a vow to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and said, "If {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} will indeed give this people into my hand, then I will devote their cities to destruction."

R.2: Then Israel made a promise to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. They said, "If {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} let us defeat these people, we will destroy their towns completely, as given over to {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}."

decisions.choice: devote to destruction: give a whole town over to God, keeping nothing for themselves
decisions.reason: The verb is the one used for a "devoted thing" in Leviticus 27:28-29: something given over to the LORD for good, which can never be bought back. In war it means the town and its people are destroyed and no plunder is taken for private use (Deuteronomy 20:16-18; Joshua 6:17-19). Israel promises not to fight this war for gain.

decisions.choice: if you will indeed give: a strong, emphatic condition
decisions.reason: The Hebrew doubles the verb ("giving you will give"), which adds emphasis: "if you will really give". Israel asks God to give the victory and promises its part in return, as Jacob's vow does (Genesis 28:20-22).

decisions.choice: my hand, I will devote: Israel speaks as one person
decisions.reason: The whole nation is "Israel" and speaks in the singular, "my hand", "I will devote". The vow is the people's together. "Into my hand" means into my power.

decisions.choice: us, we
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use "we" for the nation speaking as one, which English does not do with "I". Literal keeps the singular.

decisions.choice: destroy their towns completely, as given over to you
decisions.reason: Readable gives the sense of the term in plain words: the towns are destroyed because they are given over to God, not taken for gain. Literal and Balanced keep "devote to destruction". "Cities" in Literal; "towns" in Balanced and Readable, since these were small walled places.

records.source: וַיִּשְׁמַ֨ע יְהוָ֜ה בְּק֣וֹל יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל וַיִּתֵּן֙ אֶת־הַֽכְּנַעֲנִ֔י וַיַּחֲרֵ֥ם אֶתְהֶ֖ם וְאֶת־עָרֵיהֶ֑ם וַיִּקְרָ֥א שֵׁם־הַמָּק֖וֹם חָרְמָֽה׃פ
records.gloss: And listened Yahweh to [the] voice of Israel and gave the Canaanite[s], and he devoted to destruction them and their cities; and called [one] [the] name of the place Hormah.
pieces: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} listened to Israel's plea and handed the Canaanites over, and Israel devoted them and their towns to destruction. So the place was named Hormah.

L.3: And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} listened to the voice of Israel and gave [over] the Canaanites, and [Israel] devoted them and their cities to destruction; and [one] called the name of the place Hormah.

R.3: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} listened to Israel and let them defeat the Canaanites. The Israelites destroyed them and their towns completely, as given over to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. So that place was called Hormah, which means "Destruction."

decisions.choice: Hormah: a name made from the same word as "devote to destruction"
decisions.reason: The name sounds like the verb in this verse and verse 2, so it can be heard as "Destruction" or "Devoted place". It keeps the memory of the vow. Hormah was where Israel had been beaten back when they went up against the LORD's word (14:45); now, with the LORD's help, the same place sees their victory. Judges 1:17 tells of the naming of Hormah again, after Judah and Simeon destroyed Zephath.

decisions.choice: listened to the voice of Israel: granted what Israel asked
decisions.reason: "To listen to the voice" of someone here means to accept their request. The LORD answered the vow of verse 2.

decisions.choice: he devoted, one called: Israel did the destroying; the naming is impersonal
decisions.reason: "He devoted" has Israel, spoken of as one person, as its subject, as in verse 2. "He called" has no named subject and means "the place was called".

decisions.choice: [Israel] / Israel
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says only "he devoted". Naming Israel shows that it was the people, not the LORD, who carried out the vow.

decisions.choice: which means "Destruction"
decisions.reason: Readable gives the sense of the name so that the reader can hear how it links with the vow.

records.source: וַיִּסְע֞וּ מֵהֹ֤ר הָהָר֙ דֶּ֣רֶךְ יַם־ס֔וּף לִסְבֹ֖ב אֶת־אֶ֣רֶץ אֱד֑וֹם וַתִּקְצַ֥ר נֶֽפֶשׁ־הָעָ֖ם בַּדָּֽרֶךְ׃
records.gloss: And they set out from Hor the mountain [by the] way of [the] Sea of Reeds, to go around [the] land of Edom; and became short [the] soul of the people on the way.
pieces: They set out from Mount Hor along the road to the Red Sea, to go around the land of Edom, and on the way the people lost patience.

L.4: And they set out from Hor the mountain by the way of the Sea of Reeds, to go around the land of Edom; and the soul of the people became short on the way.

R.4: The Israelites left Mount Hor and went along the road toward the Red Sea, so that they could go around the country of Edom. But on the way the people became impatient.

decisions.choice: from Mount Hor, around Edom: the long way round
decisions.reason: Aaron had died on Mount Hor (20:22-29), and Edom had refused to let Israel pass through its land (20:14-21). So Israel had to go south and then around the edge of Edom, a long detour through hard country (Deuteronomy 2:1-8).

decisions.choice: the way of the Sea of Reeds: the road toward the gulf east of Sinai
decisions.reason: "Sea of Reeds" is the name used for the sea of the crossing (Exodus 13:18; 15:4), but it is also used for the gulf at Ezion-geber, east of the Sinai peninsula (1 Kings 9:26). Going around Edom, Israel headed south toward that gulf.

decisions.choice: the soul of the people became short: they lost patience and grew discouraged
decisions.reason: A "short soul" is the opposite of patience: people who cannot hold out any longer (Judges 10:16; 16:16). The long detour wore them down.

decisions.choice: the Red Sea
decisions.reason: As in Exodus 13:18: Balanced and Readable use the familiar name; Literal translates the Hebrew name, "Sea of Reeds".

records.heading: The bronze snake

records.source: וַיְדַבֵּ֣ר הָעָ֗ם בֵּֽאלֹהִים֮ וּבְמֹשֶׁה֒ לָמָ֤ה הֶֽעֱלִיתֻ֨נוּ֙ מִמִּצְרַ֔יִם לָמ֖וּת בַּמִּדְבָּ֑ר כִּ֣י אֵ֥ין לֶ֨חֶם֙ וְאֵ֣ין מַ֔יִם וְנַפְשֵׁ֣נוּ קָ֔צָה בַּלֶּ֖חֶם הַקְּלֹקֵֽל׃
records.gloss: And spoke the people against God and against Moses, Why have you brought us up from Egypt to die in the wilderness? For there is no bread and there is no water, and our soul loathes the bread the worthless.
pieces: The people spoke against God and against Moses: "Why have you brought us up out of Egypt to die in the wilderness? There is no food and no water, and we are sick of this pitiful food!"

L.5: And the people spoke against God and against Moses, "Why have you brought us up from Egypt to die in the wilderness? For there is no bread and there is no water, and our soul loathes the worthless bread."

R.5: The people complained against God and against Moses. They said, "Why did you bring us out of Egypt to die in this desert? There is no bread and no water. And we hate this awful food!"

decisions.choice: you have brought us up: plural, spoken to God and to Moses together
decisions.reason: "You" is plural. The people blame God and Moses at once, as the opening words of the verse say. Elsewhere the complaint is against Moses alone (20:4-5) or against God (14:2-3); here it is against both.

decisions.choice: no bread, worthless bread: no proper food, and the manna they despise
decisions.reason: The word means bread or food in general. They say there is none, and in the same breath they call the food they have "worthless": the manna, which they had already grown tired of (11:6). The complaint contradicts itself.

decisions.choice: worthless: contemptible, not worth anything
decisions.reason: The adjective is found only here. It comes from a root meaning "light" or "of little account", so it means food they treat as trash.

decisions.choice: our soul loathes: we are sick of it, we cannot stand it
decisions.reason: "Our soul" means "we ourselves", with a strong feeling of disgust (Genesis 27:46 uses the same verb).

decisions.choice: you, with no capitals
decisions.reason: This "you" is spoken to God and Moses together, so it is not written as a pronoun for God alone.

records.source: וַיְשַׁלַּ֨ח יְהוָ֜ה בָּעָ֗ם אֵ֚ת הַנְּחָשִׁ֣ים הַשְּׂרָפִ֔ים וַֽיְנַשְּׁכ֖וּ אֶת־הָעָ֑ם וַיָּ֥מָת עַם־רָ֖ב מִיִּשְׂרָאֵֽל׃
records.gloss: And sent Yahweh among the people the snakes the fiery [ones], and they bit the people; and died [a] people many from Israel.
pieces: Then {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} sent fiery snakes among the people. They bit the people, and many Israelites died.

L.6: And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} sent the fiery snakes among the people, and they bit the people; and many people of Israel died.

R.6: Then {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} sent fiery, poisonous snakes among the people. The snakes bit them, and many of the Israelites died.

decisions.choice: the fiery snakes: snakes whose bite burned, or whose color looked like fire
decisions.reason: The word added to "snakes" comes from the verb "to burn". It may describe the burning pain and fever of their poison, or a fiery color. The same word names a flying serpent in Isaiah 14:29 and 30:6, and the winged beings around God's throne in Isaiah 6:2. Deuteronomy 8:15 remembers the wilderness as a land of "fiery snakes and scorpions".

decisions.choice: the LORD sent: punishment for speaking against him
decisions.reason: The snakes come as God's answer to the people's words against him and his gift of food (verse 5). Paul recalls this event as a warning (1 Corinthians 10:9).

decisions.choice: fiery, poisonous snakes
decisions.reason: Readable adds "poisonous", since the snakes' bite killed many (this verse), whatever "fiery" refers to.

records.source: וַיָּבֹא֩ הָעָ֨ם אֶל־מֹשֶׁ֜ה וַיֹּאמְר֣וּ חָטָ֗אנוּ כִּֽי־דִבַּ֤רְנוּ בַֽיהוָה֙ וָבָ֔ךְ הִתְפַּלֵּל֙ אֶל־יְהוָ֔ה וְיָסֵ֥ר מֵעָלֵ֖ינוּ אֶת־הַנָּחָ֑שׁ וַיִּתְפַּלֵּ֥ל מֹשֶׁ֖ה בְּעַ֥ד הָעָֽם׃
records.gloss: And came the people to Moses and said, We have sinned, for we have spoken against Yahweh and against you; pray to Yahweh, and may he take away from on us the snake; and prayed Moses on behalf of the people.
pieces: The people came to Moses and said, "We sinned when we spoke against {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and against you. Pray to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} to take the snakes away from us." So Moses prayed for the people.

L.7: And the people came to Moses and said, "We have sinned, for we have spoken against {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and against you. Pray to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} may take away the snakes from us." And Moses prayed for the people.

R.7: The people came to Moses and said, "We have sinned. We spoke against {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and against you. Pray to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and ask {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} to take the snakes away from us." So Moses prayed for the people.

decisions.choice: we have sinned, for we have spoken against the LORD: the people admit their complaint was sin
decisions.reason: The people repeat the words of verse 5 ("spoke against") and name them as sin, against the LORD first and then against Moses. They ask the one they blamed to pray for them.

decisions.choice: the snake: one word standing for all the snakes
decisions.reason: The Hebrew has the singular, "the snake", used for the whole kind, as in verse 6 where the plural is used.

decisions.choice: prayed for: prayed on behalf of
decisions.reason: Moses stands between the people and God, as he did before (11:2; 14:13-19). God answers, though not by removing the snakes (verse 8).

records.source: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר יְהוָ֜ה אֶל־מֹשֶׁ֗ה עֲשֵׂ֤ה לְךָ֙ שָׂרָ֔ף וְשִׂ֥ים אֹת֖וֹ עַל־נֵ֑ס וְהָיָה֙ כָּל־הַנָּשׁ֔וּךְ וְרָאָ֥ה אֹת֖וֹ וָחָֽי׃
records.gloss: And said Yahweh to Moses, Make for yourself [a] fiery [one] and set it on [a] pole; and it will be [that] every one bitten, and he sees it, and he will live.
pieces: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} said to Moses, "Make a fiery snake and put it up on a pole. Anyone who is bitten can look at it and live."

L.8: And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said to Moses, "Make for yourself a fiery [snake] and set it on a pole; and it will be [that] everyone who is bitten and sees it will live."

R.8: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} said to Moses, "Make a model of a fiery snake and put it on top of a pole. Anyone who has been bitten can look at it and stay alive."

decisions.choice: a fiery one: a figure of the fiery snake
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says only "a fiery [one]", using the word that described the snakes in verse 6 on its own. Verse 9 shows that it was a snake made of bronze.

decisions.choice: a pole: a tall pole raised as a signal
decisions.reason: The word is used of a pole or standard set up where everyone can see it, often as a rallying sign (Isaiah 5:26; 11:12). Moses' altar was named "The LORD is my banner" with the same word (Exodus 17:15).

decisions.choice: sees it and lives: healing comes from God by trusting his word
decisions.reason: The figure does not heal by itself; God gives life to those who do what he said and look. Later, when the people burned incense to this bronze snake, King Hezekiah broke it in pieces (2 Kings 18:4). Jesus compares his own lifting up to it (John 3:14-15).

decisions.choice: a model of a fiery snake
decisions.reason: Readable makes clear that Moses is to make an image, not a living snake.

records.source: וַיַּ֤עַשׂ מֹשֶׁה֙ נְחַ֣שׁ נְחֹ֔שֶׁת וַיְשִׂמֵ֖הוּ עַל־הַנֵּ֑ס וְהָיָ֗ה אִם־נָשַׁ֤ךְ הַנָּחָשׁ֙ אֶת־אִ֔ישׁ וְהִבִּ֛יט אֶל־נְחַ֥שׁ הַנְּחֹ֖שֶׁת וָחָֽי׃
records.gloss: And made Moses [a] snake of bronze and set it on the pole; and it was [that] if had bitten the snake [a] man, and he looked to [the] snake of the bronze, and he lived.
pieces: So Moses made a bronze snake and set it on the pole. Whenever a snake had bitten someone, and that person looked at the bronze snake, they lived.

L.9: And Moses made a snake of bronze and set it on the pole; and it was [that] if the snake had bitten anyone, and {{gender:they|he}} looked to the snake of bronze, {{gender:they|he}} lived.

R.9: So Moses made a snake out of bronze and put it on the pole. After that, whenever a snake bit someone, that person could look at the bronze snake and stay alive.

decisions.choice: a snake of bronze: a play on two words that sound alike
decisions.reason: "Snake" (nachash) and "bronze" (nechoshet) sound alike in Hebrew. Bronze, a mix of copper and tin, can also shine with a reddish color like the "fiery" snakes.

decisions.choice: if ... and he looked ... and he lived: whenever this happened
decisions.reason: The verb forms describe something that kept happening: each time a person was bitten and looked, that person lived. The bronze snake stayed with Israel until Hezekiah's day (2 Kings 18:4).

decisions.choice: a man: anyone, man or woman
decisions.reason: The word often means "a man", but here it means any person the snakes bit.

records.source: וַיִּסְע֖וּ בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וַֽיַּחֲנ֖וּ בְּאֹבֹֽת׃
records.gloss: And set out [the] sons of Israel and camped in Oboth.
pieces: The {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} moved on and camped at Oboth.

L.10: And the {{gender:children|sons}} of Israel set out and camped at Oboth.

R.10: The {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} moved on and camped at a place called Oboth.

decisions.choice: Oboth: a camping place on the way around Edom
decisions.reason: Oboth is also listed among Israel's camps in 33:43-44, after Punon and before Iye-abarim. Its site is not known today.

records.source: וַיִּסְע֖וּ מֵאֹבֹ֑ת וַֽיַּחֲנ֞וּ בְּעִיֵּ֣י הָֽעֲבָרִ֗ים בַּמִּדְבָּר֙ אֲשֶׁר֙ עַל־פְּנֵ֣י מוֹאָ֔ב מִמִּזְרַ֖ח הַשָּֽׁמֶשׁ׃
records.gloss: And they set out from Oboth and camped at Iye-abarim, in the wilderness which [is] on [the] face of Moab, from [the] rising of the sun.
pieces: They set out from Oboth and camped at Iye-abarim, in the wilderness that faces Moab on the east.

L.11: And they set out from Oboth and camped at Iye-abarim, in the wilderness which [is] facing Moab, toward the rising of the sun.

R.11: Then they left Oboth and camped at Iye-abarim. It was in the desert on the east side of Moab.

decisions.choice: Iye-abarim: "the ruins of Abarim"
decisions.reason: The name means "ruins" or "heaps" of Abarim. Abarim, "the regions beyond", is the range of hills on the east side of the Dead Sea (27:12; 33:47-48). In 33:44 the camp is said to be on the border of Moab.

decisions.choice: from the rising of the sun: on the east
decisions.reason: "The rising of the sun" is the east. The camp was in the wilderness at Moab's eastern edge, still outside Moab's farmland (Deuteronomy 2:8).

records.source: מִשָּׁ֖ם נָסָ֑עוּ וַֽיַּחֲנ֖וּ בְּנַ֥חַל זָֽרֶד׃
records.gloss: From there they set out and camped in [the] wadi of Zered.
pieces: From there they moved on and camped in the Zered Valley.

L.12: From there they set out and camped in the wadi of Zered.

R.12: From there they moved on and camped in the Zered Valley.

decisions.choice: the wadi of Zered: a stream valley on Moab's southern side
decisions.reason: A wadi is a valley with a stream that often runs only in the rainy season. The Zered flows west into the south end of the Dead Sea and divided Edom from Moab. Deuteronomy 2:13-14 marks crossing it as the end of the thirty-eight years of wandering.

decisions.choice: the Zered Valley
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "wadi"; Balanced and Readable use "valley", the plain English word, here and in verses 14, 15 and 20.

records.source: מִשָּׁם֮ נָסָעוּ֒ וַֽיַּחֲנ֗וּ מֵעֵ֤בֶר אַרְנוֹן֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר בַּמִּדְבָּ֔ר הַיֹּצֵ֖א מִגְּב֣וּלהָֽאֱמֹרִ֑י כִּ֤י אַרְנוֹן֙ גְּב֣וּל מוֹאָ֔ב בֵּ֥ין מוֹאָ֖ב וּבֵ֥ין הָאֱמֹרִֽי׃
records.gloss: From there they set out and camped on [the] other side of Arnon, which [is] in the wilderness the [one] going out from [the] border of the Amorite[s]; for Arnon [is the] border of Moab, between Moab and between the Amorite[s].
pieces: From there they moved on and camped on the far side of the Arnon, in the wilderness that reaches out from the Amorite border. The Arnon is the border of Moab, between Moab and the Amorites.

L.13: From there they set out and camped on the other side of the Arnon, which [is] in the wilderness that goes out from the border of the Amorites; for the Arnon [is] the border of Moab, between Moab and the Amorites.

R.13: From there they moved on and camped on the other side of the Arnon River. They were in the desert that stretches out from the land of the Amorites. The Arnon was the border between Moab and the Amorites.

decisions.choice: the Arnon: the deep river valley between Moab and the Amorites
decisions.reason: The Arnon runs west through a deep gorge into the Dead Sea, about halfway down its eastern shore. At this time Moab lay south of it, and the Amorite kingdom of Sihon north of it (verses 24-26).

decisions.choice: the other side: probably the north side, outside Moab
decisions.reason: The text does not say which side, but it explains that the Arnon was Moab's border, and Judges 11:18 says that Israel camped beyond the Arnon and did not enter Moab's territory. Israel stayed in the wilderness at the upper Arnon, east of the settled land.

decisions.choice: the Amorites: a name for the peoples of the hill country
decisions.reason: "Amorite" is a broad name for peoples of Canaan and the land east of the Jordan (Genesis 15:16; Deuteronomy 1:7). Here it means the kingdom of Sihon (verse 21).

decisions.choice: the Arnon River
decisions.reason: Readable adds "River" so the name is clear to a reader who does not know it.

records.source: עַל־כֵּן֙ יֵֽאָמַ֔ר בְּסֵ֖פֶר מִלְחֲמֹ֣ת יְהוָ֑ה אֶת־וָהֵ֣ב בְּסוּפָ֔ה וְאֶת־הַנְּחָלִ֖ים אַרְנֽוֹן׃
records.gloss: Therefore it is said in [the] book of [the] wars of Yahweh, Waheb in Suphah, and the wadis [of] Arnon,
pieces: That is why it is said in the Book of the Wars of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}: \q "Waheb in Suphah, \q and the valleys of the Arnon,

L.14: Therefore it is said in the Book of the Wars of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, \q "Waheb in Suphah, \q and the wadis of the Arnon,

R.14: That is why the Book of the Wars of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} speaks of \q "Waheb in Suphah and the valleys of the Arnon River,

decisions.choice: the Book of the Wars of the LORD: a lost collection of songs
decisions.reason: This book is named only here. It was probably a collection of poems about the battles the LORD fought for Israel, like the Book of Jashar (Joshua 10:13; 2 Samuel 1:18). Only these few lines survive, quoted to show that the Arnon valleys belonged to Moab's border (verse 13).

decisions.choice: Waheb ... and the wadis: the quotation begins in the middle of a sentence
decisions.reason: The Hebrew marks "Waheb" and "the wadis" as objects of a verb, but the verb is not quoted. The lines may have said something like "he took" or "we passed" Waheb. The quotation is a fragment, and its main verb cannot be known.

decisions.choice: Waheb in Suphah: two places, neither of them known today
decisions.reason: Both are read as place names near the Arnon. "Suphah" may also be a common word, "storm" or "whirlwind", which would give "Waheb in a storm", perhaps a picture of the LORD coming in battle.

decisions.choice: valleys
decisions.reason: As in verse 12: Literal keeps "wadis"; Balanced and Readable use "valleys".

records.source: וְאֶ֨שֶׁד֙ הַנְּחָלִ֔ים אֲשֶׁ֥ר נָטָ֖ה לְשֶׁ֣בֶת עָ֑ר וְנִשְׁעַ֖ן לִגְב֥וּל מוֹאָֽב׃
records.gloss: and [the] slope of the wadis which extends to [the] dwelling of Ar, and leans to [the] border of Moab.
pieces: and the slope of the valleys \q that stretches toward the town of Ar \q and lies along the border of Moab."

L.15: and the slope of the wadis \q that extends to the seat of Ar \q and leans on the border of Moab."

R.15: and the hillside of the valleys that runs down to the town of Ar \q and lies along the border of Moab."

decisions.choice: the slope: the hillside running down into the valleys
decisions.reason: The word is used for the slopes at the foot of a range (Deuteronomy 3:17; Joshua 10:40). Here it is the side of the Arnon gorge.

decisions.choice: the seat of Ar: the town of Ar, the place where Ar stood
decisions.reason: Ar was a town of Moab, sometimes standing for Moab itself (verse 28; Deuteronomy 2:9, 18). "The seat of" a town means the site where it was settled.

decisions.choice: leans on the border: lies against, runs along the border
decisions.reason: The slope "leans" on Moab's border as a person leans on something: it lies right up against it. The point of the quotation is that the Arnon valleys formed Moab's edge.

records.source: וּמִשָּׁ֖ם בְּאֵ֑רָה הִ֣וא הַבְּאֵ֗ר אֲשֶׁ֨ר אָמַ֤ר יְהוָה֙ לְמֹשֶׁ֔ה אֱסֹף֙ אֶת־הָעָ֔ם וְאֶתְּנָ֥ה לָהֶ֖ם מָֽיִם׃ס
records.gloss: And from there to Beer; that [is] the well where said Yahweh to Moses, Gather the people, and let me give to them water.
pieces: From there they went on to Beer. That is the well where {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said to Moses, "Gather the people together, and I will give them water."

L.16: And from there [they went] to Beer; that [is] the well of which {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said to Moses, "Gather the people, and I will give them water."

R.16: From there they went to Beer, which means "well." This is the well where {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} told Moses, "Bring the people together, and I will give them water."

decisions.choice: Beer: a place called "Well"
decisions.reason: The name is the ordinary word for a well, as the next words explain. The place is not known today. Isaiah 15:8 names a Beer-elim in Moab, which may be the same place.

decisions.choice: gather the people, and I will give them water: water given without complaint
decisions.reason: This time the LORD gives water before the people complain, unlike at Meribah (20:2-13). The song that follows celebrates the gift.

decisions.choice: from there to Beer: the travel list goes on without a verb
decisions.reason: From here to verse 20 the stages are listed in short phrases, "from there to Beer", with "they went" understood.

decisions.choice: [they went]
decisions.reason: Literal brackets the verb English needs; Balanced and Readable supply it without brackets.

decisions.choice: which means "well"
decisions.reason: Readable gives the meaning of the name, which links it with the well in the same verse.

records.source: אָ֚ז יָשִׁ֣יר יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל אֶת־הַשִּׁירָ֖ה הַזֹּ֑את עֲלִ֥י בְאֵ֖ר עֱנוּ־לָֽהּ׃
records.gloss: Then sang Israel the song the this, Spring up, well; sing to it,
pieces: Then Israel sang this song: \q "Spring up, well! Sing out to it!

L.17: Then Israel sang this song: \q "Spring up, well! Sing to it!

R.17: Then the Israelites sang this song: \q "Bubble up, well! Sing about it!

decisions.choice: then Israel sang: the words used of the song at the sea
decisions.reason: "Then ... sang" is how the song of Moses begins after the crossing of the sea (Exodus 15:1). Here Israel sings again, over water in the wilderness.

decisions.choice: spring up, well; sing to it: the well is spoken to, then the people
decisions.reason: "Spring up" is said to the well, as if calling the water to rise. "Sing" is said to the people. The song may have been sung while digging or drawing water.

decisions.choice: sing to it: sing in answer to it, sing about it
decisions.reason: The verb can mean to answer or to sing in turns; with "to it" it means to sing over the well, greeting the water.

decisions.choice: Bubble up
decisions.reason: Readable uses a common word for water rising from the ground.

records.heading: The song of the well

records.source: בְּאֵ֞ר חֲפָר֣וּהָ שָׂרִ֗ים כָּר֨וּהָ֙ נְדִיבֵ֣י הָעָ֔ם בִּמְחֹקֵ֖ק בְּמִשְׁעֲנֹתָ֑ם וּמִמִּדְבָּ֖ר מַתָּנָֽה׃
records.gloss: well [that] dug it princes, [that] dug it nobles of the people, with [a] scepter, with their staffs; and from [the] wilderness [to] Mattanah,
pieces: the well that princes dug, that the nobles of the people dug out \q with a scepter and with their staffs." \q From the wilderness they went on to Mattanah,

L.18: the well that princes dug, that the nobles of the people dug out, \q with a scepter, with their staffs." \q And from the wilderness [they went] to Mattanah,

R.18: Leaders dug this well. The most important people dug it out \q with their scepters and their walking sticks." \q Then they went from the desert to Mattanah.

decisions.choice: princes, nobles of the people: the leading men
decisions.reason: The two words stand in parallel for the people's chief men. That they dig with their staffs of office may be a way of saying the well was opened by their command, a ceremony rather than hard digging.

decisions.choice: scepter, staffs: the rods that marked leaders
decisions.reason: The first word means a ruler's staff or one who decrees (Genesis 49:10). The second is a staff to lean on. Leaders carried such staffs as signs of their authority (17:17-18).

decisions.choice: Mattanah: a place whose name means "gift"
decisions.reason: Mattanah is a stage on the journey, not known today. The name sounds like the word for a gift, fitting after the gift of water, but the text does not draw that link.

decisions.choice: the end of the quotation before "from the wilderness"
decisions.reason: The song ends with "their staffs"; the last words go back to the list of stages begun in verse 16. The quotation marks close before them.

decisions.choice: Leaders dug this well.
decisions.reason: Readable makes the song's opening into a full sentence. Its breaks follow the Hebrew lines, one fewer than Literal.

records.source: וּמִמַּתָּנָ֖ה נַחֲלִיאֵ֑ל וּמִנַּחֲלִיאֵ֖ל בָּמֽוֹת׃
records.gloss: and from Mattanah [to] Nahaliel, and from Nahaliel [to] Bamoth,
pieces: from Mattanah to Nahaliel, from Nahaliel to Bamoth,

L.19: and from Mattanah to Nahaliel, and from Nahaliel to Bamoth,

R.19: From Mattanah they went to Nahaliel, and from Nahaliel to Bamoth.

decisions.choice: Nahaliel, Bamoth: names meaning "wadi of God" and "high places"
decisions.reason: Nahaliel means "valley of God" and Bamoth "high places", perhaps a place of worship (compare Bamoth-baal in 22:41 and Joshua 13:17). Neither place is known for certain today.

records.source: וּמִבָּמ֗וֹת הַגַּיְא֙ אֲשֶׁר֙ בִּשְׂדֵ֣ה מוֹאָ֔ב רֹ֖אשׁ הַפִּסְגָּ֑ה וְנִשְׁקָ֖פָה עַל־פְּנֵ֥י הַיְשִׁימֹֽן׃פ
records.gloss: and from Bamoth [to] the valley that [is] in [the] field of Moab, [the] top of the Pisgah; and it looks down on [the] face of the Jeshimon.
pieces: and from Bamoth to the valley in the country of Moab, by the top of Pisgah, which looks down over the wasteland of Jeshimon.

L.20: and from Bamoth to the valley that [is] in the field of Moab, [at the] top of Pisgah, which looks down on the face of the Jeshimon.

R.20: From Bamoth they went to the valley in the land of Moab, near the top of Mount Pisgah. From there you can look down on the desert wasteland.

decisions.choice: Pisgah: the ridge at the edge of the high plateau, above the Dead Sea
decisions.reason: Pisgah is the height from which Moses later saw the promised land before he died (Deuteronomy 3:27; 34:1). Balaam is taken there in 23:14.

decisions.choice: the Jeshimon: the wasteland, the desert by the Dead Sea
decisions.reason: The word means "desert" or "wasteland" and is used as the name of the barren land on the Dead Sea's shores (23:28; 1 Samuel 23:19).

decisions.choice: the field of Moab: the open country of Moab
decisions.reason: "Field" here means the open country or territory of a people, as "the field of Edom" in Genesis 32:4. This was land Moab had once held, north of the Arnon (verse 26).

decisions.choice: From there you can look down
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says that Pisgah "looks down" on the wasteland. Readable makes the picture of the view plain.

records.source: וַיִּשְׁלַ֤ח יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ מַלְאָכִ֔ים אֶל־סִיחֹ֥ן מֶֽלֶךְ־הָאֱמֹרִ֖י לֵאמֹֽר׃
records.gloss: And sent Israel messengers to Sihon, king of the Amorite[s], saying,
pieces: Then Israel sent messengers to Sihon king of the Amorites with this message:

L.21: And Israel sent messengers to Sihon, king of the Amorites, saying,

R.21: Then Israel sent messengers to Sihon, the king of the Amorites. This is what they said:

decisions.choice: Sihon, king of the Amorites: the ruler of the land north of the Arnon
decisions.reason: Sihon ruled from Heshbon (verse 26). His defeat and Og's (verses 33-35) were remembered as the LORD's great victories east of the Jordan (Deuteronomy 2:24-3:11; Psalm 136:19-20).

decisions.choice: sent messengers: the same request Israel made to Edom
decisions.reason: Israel had sent messengers with almost the same words to the king of Edom (20:14-17). Deuteronomy 2:26 says the message to Sihon was sent "with words of peace".

records.heading: Victory over Sihon and Og

records.source: אֶעְבְּרָ֣ה בְאַרְצֶ֗ךָ לֹ֤א נִטֶּה֙ בְּשָׂדֶ֣ה וּבְכֶ֔רֶם לֹ֥א נִשְׁתֶּ֖ה מֵ֣י בְאֵ֑ר בְּדֶ֤רֶךְ הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ נֵלֵ֔ךְ עַ֥ד אֲשֶֽׁר־נַעֲבֹ֖ר גְּבֻלֶֽךָ׃
records.gloss: Let me pass through your land; not we will turn aside into field or into vineyard; not we will drink water of [a] well; on [the] way of the king we will go, until that we pass your territory.
pieces: "Let us pass through your land. We will not turn off into any field or vineyard, and we will not drink water from any well. We will keep to the King's Highway until we have passed through your territory."

L.22: "Let me pass through your land. We will not turn aside into a field or into a vineyard; we will not drink water from a well; on the King's Highway we will go, until we have passed through your territory."

R.22: "Let us go through your country. We will not go into your fields or vineyards. We will not drink water from your wells. We will stay on the main road, the King's Highway, until we have gone through your land."

decisions.choice: let me pass ... we will not turn aside: the nation speaks as one, then as many
decisions.reason: The request begins in the singular, Israel speaking as one, and goes on in the plural, as in 20:17-19.

decisions.choice: the way of the king: the main road through the land east of the Jordan
decisions.reason: "The King's Highway" was the main route running north and south along the high ground east of the Dead Sea, as in 20:17.

decisions.choice: fields, vineyards, wells: the land's food and water
decisions.reason: Israel promises not to take crops, fruit or water, which in dry country were worth guarding. In 20:19 they even offered to pay for water.

decisions.choice: Let us
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use "us" from the start, since the nation is meant. Literal keeps the singular.

records.source: וְלֹא־נָתַ֨ן סִיחֹ֣ן אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵל֮ עֲבֹ֣ר בִּגְבֻלוֹ֒ וַיֶּאֱסֹ֨ף סִיחֹ֜ן אֶת־כָּל־עַמּ֗וֹ וַיֵּצֵ֞א לִקְרַ֤את יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ הַמִּדְבָּ֔רָה וַיָּבֹ֖א יָ֑הְצָה וַיִּלָּ֖חֶם בְּיִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃
records.gloss: And not did allow Sihon Israel to pass through his territory; and gathered Sihon all his people and went out to meet Israel to the wilderness, and came to Jahaz and fought against Israel.
pieces: But Sihon would not let Israel pass through his territory. He gathered all his forces and marched out into the wilderness against Israel. When he reached Jahaz, he fought against Israel.

L.23: And Sihon did not allow Israel to pass through his territory; and Sihon gathered all his people and went out to meet Israel in the wilderness, and he came to Jahaz and fought against Israel.

R.23: But Sihon would not let Israel go through his land. He called together his whole army and went out into the desert to fight Israel. He came to Jahaz, and there he attacked the Israelites.

decisions.choice: his people: his fighting men
decisions.reason: "People" here means the men who could fight, the army, as often in accounts of battle (20:20).

decisions.choice: went out to meet Israel: went out to fight them
decisions.reason: "To meet" someone with an army means to march out against them, as Edom did in 20:20.

decisions.choice: Jahaz: a town on the plateau north of the Arnon
decisions.reason: Jahaz is named again in this battle in Deuteronomy 2:32 and Judges 11:20, and later as a town of Reuben and of Moab (Joshua 13:18; Isaiah 15:4). Its exact site is not certain.

decisions.choice: forces, army
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the sense of "people" in this battle: his fighting men.

records.source: וַיַּכֵּ֥הוּ יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל לְפִי־חָ֑רֶב וַיִּירַ֨שׁ אֶת־אַרְצ֜וֹ מֵֽאַרְנֹ֗ן עַד־יַבֹּק֙ עַד־בְּנֵ֣י עַמּ֔וֹן כִּ֣י עַ֔ז גְּב֖וּל בְּנֵ֥י עַמּֽוֹן׃
records.gloss: And struck him Israel by [the] mouth of [the] sword and took possession of his land from Arnon to Jabbok, to [the] sons of Ammon; for strong [was the] border of [the] sons of Ammon.
pieces: Israel defeated him in battle and took possession of his land from the Arnon to the Jabbok, as far as the Ammonites, for the Ammonite border was strongly held.

L.24: And Israel struck him with the edge of the sword and took possession of his land from the Arnon to the Jabbok, as far as the sons of Ammon; for the border of the sons of Ammon [was] strong.

R.24: But the Israelites defeated Sihon in battle. They took over his land from the Arnon River to the Jabbok River, as far as the land of the Ammonites. They stopped there because the Ammonite border was well defended.

decisions.choice: by the mouth of the sword: in battle, with the sword
decisions.reason: The sword is pictured as a mouth that devours (2 Samuel 2:26). The phrase means they defeated him by fighting, killing those who fought.

decisions.choice: from the Arnon to the Jabbok: the land between the two rivers
decisions.reason: The Jabbok flows west into the Jordan north of the Dead Sea, where Jacob wrestled at its ford (Genesis 32:23). The land between the Arnon and the Jabbok became the territory of Reuben and Gad (chapter 32; Joshua 13:15-28).

decisions.choice: for the border of the Ammonites was strong
alternatives: for Jazer was the border of the Ammonites
decisions.reason: The Hebrew text says the Ammonite border was "strong", that is, well defended, which explains why Israel stopped there. The ancient Greek translation reads "for Jazer was the border of the Ammonites", taking a word that looks very like "strong" as the town of Jazer (verse 32). Deuteronomy 2:37 says instead that Israel did not go near the Ammonites' land because the LORD forbade it.

decisions.choice: They stopped there because
decisions.reason: Readable spells out how the last clause connects: the strong border is why the conquest ended at the Ammonites.

records.source: וַיִּקַּח֙ יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל אֵ֥ת כָּל־הֶעָרִ֖ים הָאֵ֑לֶּה וַיֵּ֤שֶׁב יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ בְּכָל־עָרֵ֣י הָֽאֱמֹרִ֔י בְּחֶשְׁבּ֖וֹן וּבְכָל־בְּנֹתֶֽיהָ׃
records.gloss: And took Israel all the cities the these, and dwelt Israel in all [the] cities of the Amorite[s], in Heshbon and in all its daughters.
pieces: Israel took all these towns and settled in all the towns of the Amorites, in Heshbon and all its villages.

L.25: And Israel took all these cities, and Israel lived in all the cities of the Amorites, in Heshbon and in all its daughters.

R.25: Israel captured all these towns and lived in them. They lived in all the Amorite towns, including Heshbon and all the villages around it.

decisions.choice: its daughters: the villages that belonged to the town
decisions.reason: A town's "daughters" are the smaller settlements around it that depended on it (Joshua 15:45; Judges 11:26).

decisions.choice: Heshbon: Sihon's royal city
decisions.reason: Heshbon stood on the high plateau east of the north end of the Dead Sea. It was later given to Reuben and then counted among the Levites' towns (32:37; Joshua 21:39).

records.source: כִּ֣י חֶשְׁבּ֔וֹן עִ֗יר סִיחֹ֛ן מֶ֥לֶךְ הָאֱמֹרִ֖י הִ֑וא וְה֣וּא נִלְחַ֗ם בְּמֶ֤לֶךְ מוֹאָב֙ הָֽרִאשׁ֔וֹן וַיִּקַּ֧ח אֶת־כָּל־אַרְצ֛וֹ מִיָּד֖וֹ עַד־אַרְנֹֽן׃
records.gloss: For Heshbon [was the] city of Sihon, king of the Amorite[s], it; and he had fought against [the] king of Moab the former and taken all his land from his hand as far as Arnon.
pieces: Heshbon was the city of Sihon king of the Amorites. He had fought against the former king of Moab and taken all his land from him, as far as the Arnon.

L.26: For Heshbon [was] the city of Sihon, king of the Amorites, and he had fought against the former king of Moab and taken all his land out of his hand, as far as the Arnon.

R.26: Heshbon was the capital city of Sihon, the king of the Amorites. Before this, Sihon had fought against the king who ruled Moab then, and taken all his land as far south as the Arnon River.

decisions.choice: and he had fought: something that happened before Israel came
decisions.reason: The verse steps back to explain how Heshbon, once Moab's, had become Sihon's. This prepares for the song in verses 27-30, which tells of the fire that went out from Heshbon against Moab.

decisions.choice: the former king of Moab: the king of Moab before the present one
decisions.reason: The king Sihon fought is not named. He ruled Moab before Balak, who was king when Israel arrived (22:4).

decisions.choice: from his hand: out of his power, from his rule
decisions.reason: "Hand" stands for power and control, as in verse 2.

decisions.choice: the capital city, as far south as
decisions.reason: Readable makes explicit what the context implies: Heshbon was the city Sihon ruled from (verse 34), and the land he took ran south to the Arnon (verse 13).

records.source: עַל־כֵּ֛ן יֹאמְר֥וּ הַמֹּשְׁלִ֖ים בֹּ֣אוּ חֶשְׁבּ֑וֹן תִּבָּנֶ֥ה וְתִכּוֹנֵ֖ן עִ֥יר סִיחֽוֹן׃
records.gloss: Therefore say those speaking proverbs, Come [to] Heshbon; let be built and let be established [the] city of Sihon.
pieces: That is why the poets say, "Come to Heshbon! \q Let the city of Sihon be rebuilt and made strong again!

L.27: Therefore those who speak in proverbs say, "Come to Heshbon! \q Let the city of Sihon be built and be established!

R.27: That is why the poets say, "Come to Heshbon! \q Let Sihon's city be built up again!

decisions.choice: those who speak in proverbs: poets, singers of sayings and songs
decisions.reason: The word is used for someone who makes up a short saying or a mocking song (Ezekiel 16:44). Balaam's oracles use the noun from the same root (23:7).

decisions.choice: come to Heshbon, let it be rebuilt: a taunt over a city that has been brought down
alternatives: a call to rebuild Heshbon for Israel
decisions.reason: The song may be an old Amorite song of victory over Moab (verses 28-29), used now to celebrate Israel's victory over the Amorites. "Let it be rebuilt" can then be heard as a taunt: Sihon's proud city, which once burned Moab, is now itself in ruins. It can also be read as a call to Israel to rebuild Heshbon and settle there. Jeremiah 48:45-46 takes up lines of this song against Moab.

decisions.choice: rebuilt and made strong again
decisions.reason: Balanced makes clear that the city is to be built again after its fall; "established" means made firm and secure.

records.source: כִּי־אֵשׁ֙ יָֽצְאָ֣ה מֵֽחֶשְׁבּ֔וֹן לֶהָבָ֖ה מִקִּרְיַ֣ת סִיחֹ֑ן אָֽכְלָה֙ עָ֣ר מוֹאָ֔ב בַּעֲלֵ֖י בָּמ֥וֹת אַרְנֹֽן׃
records.gloss: For fire went out from Heshbon, flame from [the] town of Sihon; it consumed Ar of Moab, [the] lords of [the] heights of Arnon.
pieces: For fire went out from Heshbon, \q a flame from the city of Sihon. \q It burned up Ar of Moab, \q the lords of the heights of the Arnon.

L.28: For fire went out from Heshbon, \q flame from the town of Sihon; \q it consumed Ar of Moab, \q the lords of the heights of the Arnon.

R.28: Fire came out of Heshbon, \q flames from the city of Sihon. \q They burned up the town of Ar in Moab \q and the rulers of the hills by the Arnon.

decisions.choice: fire, flame: war that destroys like fire
decisions.reason: The fire stands for Sihon's armies going out from his city and destroying Moab (verse 26), as war is often pictured as fire (Amos 1:4; 2:2).

decisions.choice: the lords of the heights of the Arnon: the rulers or people of the hill towns above the Arnon
alternatives: it swallowed up the heights of the Arnon
decisions.reason: "Lords" can mean the owners or citizens of a place (Judges 9:2). "Heights" may be high places of worship or simply the hills above the gorge. The ancient Greek translation reads "it swallowed up the heights of the Arnon", from a word that looks much the same.

decisions.choice: Ar of Moab: a town of Moab standing for the land
decisions.reason: As in verse 15, Ar was a town of Moab near the Arnon, sometimes standing for the whole land (Deuteronomy 2:9).

records.source: אוֹי־לְךָ֣ מוֹאָ֔ב אָבַ֖דְתָּ עַם־כְּמ֑וֹשׁ נָתַ֨ן בָּנָ֤יו פְּלֵיטִם֙ וּבְנֹתָ֣יו בַּשְּׁבִ֔ית לְמֶ֥לֶךְ אֱמֹרִ֖י סִיחֽוֹן׃
records.gloss: Woe to you, Moab; you have perished, people of Chemosh; he has given his sons [as] fugitives and his daughters into captivity, to [the] king of [the] Amorite[s], Sihon.
pieces: How terrible for you, Moab! \q You are destroyed, people of Chemosh! \q He has let his sons become refugees and his daughters captives \q of Sihon king of the Amorites.

L.29: Woe to you, Moab! \q You have perished, people of Chemosh! \q He has given his sons as fugitives, and his daughters into captivity, \q to the king of the Amorites, Sihon.

R.29: How terrible for you, Moab! \q You people who worship Chemosh are destroyed! \q Your god let his sons run away and his daughters be taken captive \q by Sihon, the king of the Amorites.

decisions.choice: Chemosh: the god of Moab
decisions.reason: Chemosh was the chief god of the Moabites (Judges 11:24; 1 Kings 11:7). The song calls Moab his people and pictures him unable to save them.

decisions.choice: he has given his sons: Chemosh handed over his own people
decisions.reason: "He" is Chemosh. His "sons" and "daughters" are the people of Moab. The song mocks a god who gave up his own children to Sihon. Jeremiah 48:46 repeats these words against Moab.

decisions.choice: woe to you: a cry of grief or doom
decisions.reason: "Woe" is a cry over a disaster that has come or is coming (1 Samuel 4:7-8; Isaiah 6:5).

decisions.choice: How terrible for you
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable avoid the old word "woe", which is little used in modern speech; Literal keeps it.

decisions.choice: Your god
decisions.reason: Readable names the subject of "he has given", which the Hebrew leaves to the reader.

records.source: וַנִּירָ֛ם אָבַ֥ד חֶשְׁבּ֖וֹן עַד־דִּיב֑וֹן וַנַּשִּׁ֣ים עַד־נֹ֔פַח אֲשֶׁ֖רׄעַד־מֵֽידְבָֽא׃
records.gloss: And we shot at them; perished Heshbon as far as Dibon; and we laid waste as far as Nophah, which [is] as far as Medeba.
pieces: But we shot at them; Heshbon is destroyed as far as Dibon. \q We laid the land waste as far as Nophah, \q which reaches to Medeba."

L.30: But we shot at them; Heshbon has perished as far as Dibon, \q and we laid [them] waste as far as Nophah, \q which [reaches] to Medeba."

R.30: But we shot arrows at them. Heshbon is ruined all the way to Dibon. \q We destroyed the land as far as Nophah, near Medeba."

decisions.choice: we shot at them ... which reaches to Medeba: a hard verse, read as the Hebrew text stands
alternatives: their yoke has perished from Heshbon to Dibon
with fire as far as Medeba
decisions.reason: The words of this verse are difficult. The first verb is read here as "we shot at them", but the same letters could mean "their yoke" or "their lamp" ("their rule has perished"). In "which [reaches] to Medeba" the Hebrew scribes marked a letter as doubtful, and with one letter changed it reads "fire": "we laid waste ... with fire to Medeba", as the Samaritan text and the ancient Greek translation take it.

decisions.choice: we: the victors who sing the song
decisions.reason: "We" are the conquerors who sing, Sihon's men in the old song, or Israel as it uses the song after beating Sihon (verse 27). "Them" are the people of Moab, or the towns.

decisions.choice: Dibon, Nophah, Medeba: towns on the plateau north of the Arnon
decisions.reason: Dibon lay just north of the Arnon, and Medeba farther north, near Heshbon (32:3; Joshua 13:9). The places named sweep across the whole land Sihon had taken. Nophah is not known today.

decisions.choice: laid [them] waste
decisions.reason: Literal brackets the object English needs; Balanced and Readable say "the land" without brackets.

decisions.choice: near Medeba
decisions.reason: Readable folds the last line into the one before it and gives its sense in two words.

records.source: וַיֵּ֨שֶׁב֙ יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל בְּאֶ֖רֶץ הָאֱמֹרִֽי׃
records.gloss: And dwelt Israel in [the] land of the Amorite[s].
pieces: So Israel settled in the land of the Amorites.

L.31: And Israel lived in the land of the Amorites.

R.31: So the Israelites lived in the land of the Amorites.

decisions.choice: Israel lived there: the end of the song's account
decisions.reason: After the song the story returns to verse 25: Israel settled in the conquered land, the first land it held east of the Jordan.

records.source: וַיִּשְׁלַ֤ח מֹשֶׁה֙ לְרַגֵּ֣ל אֶת־יַעְזֵ֔ר וַֽיִּלְכְּד֖וּ בְּנֹתֶ֑יהָ וַיּ֖וֹרֶשׁ אֶת־הָאֱמֹרִ֥י אֲשֶׁר־שָֽׁם׃
records.gloss: And sent Moses to spy out Jazer, and they captured its daughters and dispossessed the Amorite[s] who [were] there.
pieces: Moses sent men to scout out Jazer, and they captured its villages and drove out the Amorites who lived there.

L.32: And Moses sent [men] to spy out Jazer, and they captured its daughters and dispossessed the Amorites who [were] there.

R.32: Moses sent men to explore the area around the town of Jazer. The Israelites captured the villages there and forced out the Amorites who lived in them.

decisions.choice: Jazer: a town north of Heshbon, near the Ammonite border
decisions.reason: Jazer later belonged to Gad and was known for its grazing land (32:1, 35; Joshua 13:25).

decisions.choice: dispossessed: the word as the Hebrew scribes read it
decisions.reason: The written letters of the Hebrew text would give "and he took possession of" the Amorites' land; the scribes' reading, followed here, is "and he dispossessed" the Amorites. The meaning is much the same: Israel drove them out and took their place.

decisions.choice: its daughters: the villages around Jazer
decisions.reason: As in verse 25.

decisions.choice: [men], men
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says only that Moses "sent". The next verb, "they captured", shows that those he sent took part in the attack.

records.source: וַיִּפְנוּ֙ וַֽיַּעֲל֔וּ דֶּ֖רֶךְ הַבָּשָׁ֑ן וַיֵּצֵ֣א עוֹג֩ מֶֽלֶךְ־הַבָּשָׁ֨ן לִקְרָאתָ֜ם ה֧וּא וְכָל־עַמּ֛וֹ לַמִּלְחָמָ֖ה אֶדְרֶֽעִי׃
records.gloss: And they turned and went up [by the] way of the Bashan; and came out Og, king of the Bashan, to meet them, he and all his people, for battle [at] Edrei.
pieces: Then they turned and went up along the road to Bashan, and Og king of Bashan marched out against them with all his army to fight at Edrei.

L.33: And they turned and went up by the way of Bashan; and Og, king of Bashan, came out to meet them, he and all his people, for battle at Edrei.

R.33: Then the Israelites turned and went north along the road to Bashan. Og, the king of Bashan, came out with his whole army to fight them at Edrei.

decisions.choice: Bashan and Og: the land and king north of the Jabbok
decisions.reason: Bashan was the rich high country east of the Sea of Galilee, known for its cattle and oaks (Deuteronomy 32:14; Isaiah 2:13). Og was its king, remembered as the last of the giant Rephaim (Deuteronomy 3:11).

decisions.choice: Edrei: a town on Bashan's southern edge
decisions.reason: Edrei was one of Og's royal cities (Deuteronomy 1:4; Joshua 12:4), on the southern edge of Bashan.

decisions.choice: went up: climbed north toward the higher land
decisions.reason: "Went up" fits the road north from the Jabbok into the high plateau of Bashan.

decisions.choice: army
decisions.reason: As in verse 23, "his people" in battle means his fighting men.

records.source: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר יְהוָ֤ה אֶל־מֹשֶׁה֙ אַל־תִּירָ֣א אֹת֔וֹ כִּ֣י בְיָדְךָ֞ נָתַ֧תִּי אֹת֛וֹ וְאֶת־כָּל־עַמּ֖וֹ וְאֶת־אַרְצ֑וֹ וְעָשִׂ֣יתָ לּ֔וֹ כַּאֲשֶׁ֣ר עָשִׂ֗יתָ לְסִיחֹן֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ הָֽאֱמֹרִ֔י אֲשֶׁ֥ר יוֹשֵׁ֖ב בְּחֶשְׁבּֽוֹן׃
records.gloss: And said Yahweh to Moses, Do not fear him, for into your hand I have given him and all his people and his land; and you will do to him as you did to Sihon, king of the Amorite[s], who dwelt in Heshbon.
pieces: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} said to Moses, "Do not be afraid of him, for I have handed him over to you, with all his army and his land. Do to him what you did to Sihon king of the Amorites, who ruled in Heshbon."

L.34: And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said to Moses, "Do not fear him, for into your hand I have given him and all his people and his land; and you will do to him as you did to Sihon, king of the Amorites, who lived in Heshbon."

R.34: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} said to Moses, "Do not be afraid of him. I am giving him, his whole army and his land to you. Do to him what you did to Sihon, the Amorite king who ruled in Heshbon."

decisions.choice: I have given: as good as done
decisions.reason: The verb is in the form for a finished act. The LORD speaks of the victory as already given before the battle is fought (Joshua 6:2; 8:1).

decisions.choice: into your hand: into your power
decisions.reason: As in verse 2, "hand" stands for power. The words come back in Deuteronomy 3:2.

decisions.choice: all his people: his fighting men and his whole nation
decisions.reason: "People" here takes in his army (verse 33) and, as verse 35 shows, all who belonged to him.

decisions.choice: you will do: a command as well as a promise
decisions.reason: The verb can be heard both as what Moses will do and as what he is told to do.

decisions.choice: Do to him; who ruled in Heshbon
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the command sense, and "ruled" for "lived", since Sihon lived in Heshbon as its king.

records.source: וַיַּכּ֨וּ אֹת֤וֹ וְאֶת־בָּנָיו֙ וְאֶת־כָּל־עַמּ֔וֹ עַד־בִּלְתִּ֥י הִשְׁאִֽיר־ל֖וֹ שָׂרִ֑יד וַיִּֽירְשׁ֖וּ אֶת־אַרְצֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: And they struck him and his sons and all his people until not was left to him a survivor; and they took possession of his land.
pieces: So they struck down Og, his sons and all his army, until not one survivor was left, and they took possession of his land.

L.35: And they struck him and his sons and all his people, until no survivor was left to him; and they took possession of his land.

R.35: So the Israelites killed Og, his sons and his whole army. No one was left alive. Then they took over his land.

decisions.choice: struck: struck down, defeated and killed
decisions.reason: The verb means to strike, and in battle to strike down. With "until no survivor was left" it means the killing of his forces.

decisions.choice: until no survivor was left: told again in Deuteronomy 3
decisions.reason: Deuteronomy 3:3-6 tells the same victory and says Og's towns were devoted to destruction as Sihon's were. The land of Sihon and Og became the inheritance of Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh (32:33).

decisions.choice: Og
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name Og, since the chapter has spoken of two kings.
